The Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) is a globally abundant dabbling duck whose life-history traits have been extensively documented across its broad Holarctic range. Fresh eggs in this species typically weigh approximately 50.6 grams [Ww0 = approximately 50.6 grams], a value consistent with the constraints of female body size and the demands of precocial development. Laboratory incubation experiments conducted at a stable temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] indicate that embryos complete their development and hatch after an average incubation period of 25.5 days [ab = 25.5 days], a duration that aligns closely with reports for other temperate-nesting anatids. This thermal dependence of embryonic growth underscores the importance of consistent maternal brooding behavior, particularly during the early stages of egg attendance when nest attendance is most continuous. The resulting hatchlings emerge at a wet body mass of roughly 32.4 grams [Wwb = roughly 32.4 grams], a modest neonatal mass that reflects the substantial yolk reserves already absorbed during the late stages of incubation and positions the downy young for immediate exotrophic transition under parental guidance, consistent with the precocial developmental strategy typical of the Anatidae.

Reproductive output in the Mallard is shaped by a trade-off between clutch size and the number of nesting attempts per season. Females typically produce a single clutch of approximately 14 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = approximately 14 eggs per nesting attempt], and under optimal conditions may initiate up to two replacement clutches annually [F_R_i = up to two replacement clutches annually] following nest failure, a strategy that buffers against high predation pressure on ground nests. This reproductive schedule yields a maximum annual reproductive rate that is modest compared to many passerines of equivalent body size but typical for a waterfowl species with substantial per-offspring investment. The post-hatching period is characterized by rapid somatic growth; ducklings achieve the capacity for sustained flight at approximately 55 days after hatching [tx = approximately 55 days after hatching], an interval that marks the completion of wing feather development and the onset of nutritional independence from the brood-rearing female. This fledging duration reflects the energetic demands of attaining a body mass capable of powered flight.

Asymptotic body mass in the Mallard exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a pattern common among anatids where males typically attain larger final sizes than females. Adult females reach a mean ultimate wet weight of approximately 1099.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 1099.5 grams], whereas adult males achieve a substantially greater final mass averaging 1206.5 grams [Wwi = 1206.5 grams]. This size disparity is linked to the males' investment in competitive displays and territorial defense during the breeding season, while females may face energetic constraints imposed by egg production and the demands of extended incubation. The species' growth trajectory follows a decelerating curve typical of large-bodied waterfowl, with most structural growth completed well before the onset of winter migration. These mass values have been confirmed through extensive field studies across multiple populations, exhibiting relatively low inter-population variation despite the species' vast geographic range, suggesting a canalized adult body size under strong stabilizing selection for optimal flight efficiency and thermal insulation.

The Mallard's maturation timeline follows a pattern common to many temperate-nesting ducks, with a clear distinction between the attainment of sexual dimorphism and the onset of reproductive competence. Field studies indicate that puberty, defined by the initiation of gametogenesis and development of secondary sexual characteristics, is reached at approximately 165 days after hatching [tp = approximately 165 days after hatching]. This developmental milestone coincides with the post-juvenile molt and the acquisition of definitive adult plumage, which is particularly striking in males. However, despite the relatively early onset of gonadal activity, most individuals do not successfully produce their first brood until roughly one year after birth [tR = roughly one year after birth]. This delay between physiological maturity and first successful reproduction is common in waterfowl and is likely driven by the need to acquire breeding experience, establish a pair bond, and secure a suitable nesting territory. The extended interval, which corresponds closely to a 365-day period (365 days since birth) [tR = 365 days since birth], reflects the strongly seasonal nature of temperate breeding systems where a single annual window is available.

Maximum longevity in the Mallard is notably high for a bird of its body mass, with band-recovery analyses and captive records indicating a potential lifespan of up to 29.1 years [am = up to 29.1 years]. This remarkable longevity is among the highest documented for any dabbling duck species and likely reflects a combination of factors including a relatively low adult mortality rate once individuals attain breeding age, the ability to exploit a diverse and abundant food supply across a wide variety of wetlands, and strong anti-predator behaviors including rapid flight and cryptic nesting. The contrast between the species' high annual reproductive output and its extended potential lifespan places it on the slow end of the life-history continuum when compared to many smaller-bodied, shorter-lived waterfowl species. It is worth noting that while the species achieves 29.1 years [am = 29.1 years] as a maximum, the median life expectancy in wild populations is considerably shorter, typically ranging from one to three years, with most mortality concentrated in the first year of life during the vulnerable fledgling and juvenile stages before the attainment of sexual maturity.
